background: Throughput scheduling asks which jobs can be completed by their due dates when the machine cannot process everything on time. In the single-machine model with release dates, each job has an availability time, a processing requirement, and a deadline; the algorithm chooses a feasible nonpreemptive schedule and maximizes the number or total weight of on-time jobs. The case without release dates has classical polynomial or pseudo-polynomial algorithms, but release dates make the geometry much harder because feasible intervals for jobs interact over time. Sgall highlighted the constant-processing-time regime as a natural open frontier: if every job has processing time at most a fixed constant $c$, is the problem polynomial? Mnich and van Bevern reframed this as a parameterized-complexity question in $p_{\max}$. This formulation is useful because an FPT or XP algorithm would be evidence for tractability at every fixed $c$, while W-hardness would explain why even bounded processing times do not tame release-date throughput scheduling.
open_problem: Determine whether $1|r_j,p_j\le c|\sum U_j$ is polynomial-time solvable for each fixed $c$, and settle the weighted constant-$c$ case; equivalently, classify $1|r_j|\sum U_j$ and $1|r_j|\sum w_jU_j$ parameterized by $p_{\max}$.
known_results: Without release dates, $1||\sum U_j$ is polynomial-time solvable by the Moore-Hodgson algorithm, while $1||\sum w_jU_j$ is weakly NP-hard but pseudo-polynomial. With release dates and arbitrary processing times, throughput scheduling is hard. Sgall asked whether the unweighted release-date case is polynomial for every fixed processing-time bound $c$, and whether the weighted case is NP-hard for fixed $c$. Mnich and van Bevern state the parameterized version as Open Problem 3 and note that, at the time, even containment in XP for parameter $p_{\max}$ was open. Hermelin et al. give FPT algorithms when two of three diversity parameters are simultaneously bounded: distinct due dates, distinct processing times, and distinct weights. The single-parameter $p_{\max}$ question remains the clean gap.

progress.summary: The problem is understood for no release dates and for combinations of multiple diversity parameters, but not for $p_{\max}$ alone. The parameterized classification remains open in the dataset.

counterexample_rationale: This is a complexity-classification problem. Search may find reductions or algorithmic patterns, but a finite counterexample cannot resolve it.
alphaevolve_rationale: Program search can test dynamic-programming state compressions for small $p_{\max}$ and discover reduction gadgets. The final result needs a proof of FPT/XP membership or parameterized hardness.

literature.synthesis: The key difficulty is that small processing times do not obviously bound the number of relevant time configurations once release dates and due dates are arbitrary. Classical pseudo-polynomial algorithms exploit total processing time or integer time horizons, but FPT in $p_{\max}$ would require compressing the schedule without depending exponentially on horizon length or the number of distinct release/deadline values. Hermelin-style diversity-parameter algorithms show that the problem becomes tractable when more structure is bounded, but they do not isolate $p_{\max}$. The open problem therefore sits exactly at the boundary between numerical boundedness and combinatorial time-window complexity.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Try interval-DP formulations that use bounded job lengths but avoid dependence on the number of distinct time points. For hardness, attempt reductions that encode choices through release/deadline windows while all processing times are drawn from $\{1,\ldots,p_{\max}\}$.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: An FPT claim must run in $f(p_{\max})\mathrm{poly}(|I|)$ time with binary-encoded dates and weights. A polynomial-time result for each fixed $c$ should make the exponent independent of $c$ if claimed as FPT; an $n^{f(c)}$ algorithm is only XP.
